This paper introduces DiffTry (Differential Retries), a lightweight, stateless mechanism that prioritizes high-value microservice requests during overload by assigning different retry-attempt limits to different transaction classes, requiring no overload sensing or service coordination. The approach addresses key weaknesses of conventional retries, which fail to protect valuable transactions and can trigger performance-degrading "retry storms," and it also defends against attackers who flood systems with cheap low-priority requests to cause mass rejection of legitimate traffic. The authors develop an analytical model for two services in tandem and generalize it to arbitrary networks, proving that their iterative solution method always converges and establishing uniqueness guarantees for DAG-structured workflows along with monotonicity results showing success rates improve with retry limits. In illustrative overload scenarios, DiffTry reduces high-priority rejection to around 15% and lets high-priority transactions account for roughly 85% of successful completions even when each class contributes half the input load, yielding about a 70% throughput improvement. The authors validate their predictions through simulation and a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry runs as a drop-in service-mesh plugin needing no application changes and produces measured rejection rates that closely match the analysis.

summary_responses.response: The FAA has adopted a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes, effective November 18, 2026, prompted by reports of low clearance in the right wing between fuel line couplings, a harness support bracket clip-nut, the hydraulic system, and the fuel vent tube. The directive requires rectifying these low-clearance conditions and inspecting for adequate clearance, since the defects could create an ignition source in the fuel tank during a lightning strike. The AD stems from a Transport Canada directive (CF-2025-49) and follows an NPRM that drew support from five commenters, while two others raised concerns. In response, the FAA declined to issue an emergency AD or reopen the comment period, explaining that the compliance times were adequate, the condition would not cause fuel starvation, and the incorporated materials met the "reasonably available" standard. The FAA estimates the AD affects 60 U.S.-registered airplanes at a cost of $2,693 per aircraft for required actions, with additional possible on-condition costs, though some expenses may be covered under warranty.

summary_responses.subtopic: Public Administration, Labor Policy & Family Leave
summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in order to incorporate statutory amendments enacted in January 2021 and December 2023. The rule broadens FMLA eligibility by making virtually all federal civilian service (including temporary or intermittent work) and certain honorable active military service count toward the required 12 months of qualifying service, which also affects eligibility for paid parental leave. It clarifies that annual and sick leave earned under authorities outside of title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, and it excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees—those covered by a separate leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421—from title 5 FMLA coverage. These changes codify existing guidance previously issued through two OPM memoranda to agency heads. The rule takes effect December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026, in which case OPM will withdraw the affected provisions and issue a proposed rulemaking instead.
